title: Feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings

narration: Priya gives a status update to her team.
beats.visual_intent: Presenter introduces the moment; behind her, Priya mid-update, her manager delivers the vague line

grounding.claim: a manager telling someone to communicate better without naming what they said or did is a common example of vague feedback

beats.visual_intent: replay of the same update, visually identical to the first, undercutting the idea that the feedback worked

grounding.claim: vague feedback does not identify which specific action to repeat, change or stop, so it tends not to change what happens next time

narration: By the end of this, you can fix that.
That's what changes what happens next.
beats.visual_intent: Presenter to camera states the promise, no scene behind her yet

narration: It's a verdict on who she is,
beats.visual_intent: the vague phrase breaks into two labels: a character verdict and a specific action, the verdict highlighted as the wrong read

grounding.claim: feedback aimed at a person's character rather than their behaviour is commonly heard as a judgement of identity and tends to trigger defensiveness

narration: A behaviour is what she actually said or did.
Here: the timeline and the blockers,
on_screen: Behaviour: what was said or done
beats.visual_intent: the character-verdict label fades; a specific behaviour label pulled from the actual update replaces it

grounding.claim: a behaviour means an observable action, as distinct from an inferred trait, motive or label
the first part of feedback names a specific, observable behaviour rather than a trait or character judgement

narration: Vague feedback like this doesn't say what to change.
It only makes her feel judged.
She still won't know what to do differently.
beats.visual_intent: the vague verdict sits next to a question mark reading 'what do I do differently', a small frown icon beside it

grounding.claim: because vague or character-directed feedback does not identify a specific, repeatable action, it tends not to change what the person does next time, even when it changes how they feel

beats.misconception: if feedback states the problem clearly and firmly, it will change what the person does next time

narration: "Because the timeline and blockers were mixed in,
I couldn't tell what was blocking us."
beats.visual_intent: the behaviour label grows a second line underneath: the concrete impact, joined to it by a short connecting arrow

grounding.claim: describing the concrete impact of a behaviour helps the other person understand why it matters, not only that someone is unhappy

narration: "What got left out, from your side?"
beats.visual_intent: a third line appears under behaviour and impact, completing a three-part on-screen sequence

grounding.claim: ending feedback with a question invites the other person to add context and take part in deciding what happens next
a closing question that asks what the other person noticed turns the exchange into a two-way conversation rather than a verdict

on_screen: Verdict ends it. Question starts it.
beats.visual_intent: split screen: a closed-door icon over the verdict line, an open-door icon over the question line

grounding.claim: a feedback conversation that only states a verdict can feel one-sided to the receiver even when the content is accurate
inviting the other person's view before agreeing on a next step increases the chance the change is something they can actually do

beats.visual_intent: the three-part shape assembles fully on screen and holds for a beat, as the reusable sequence

grounding.claim: a widely taught way to structure workplace feedback is in three parts, in this order: behaviour, impact, question

narration: A: "You're disorganized, you need to communicate better."
B: "When the blockers were mixed into the timeline,
I couldn't tell what was blocking us.
Which one changes next week's update?
beats.visual_intent: two feedback lines appear side by side, A the verdict, B the three-part shape; narration pauses before the reveal

recall.prompt: Which reply is more likely to change next week's update?

narration: It names the behaviour, the impact, and asks.
A hands down a verdict, so nothing moves.
on_screen: B: names it, shows impact, asks
beats.visual_intent: B highlighted and broken into its three labelled parts; A fades with the question mark from earlier

recall.why_wrong_tempting: A feels direct and honest, and the person often reacts right away, but reacting isn't the same as knowing what to change

grounding.claim: the first line feels direct and even changes how someone feels in the moment, but it does not identify a specific, repeatable action

narration: "When the blockers were mixed into the timeline,
I couldn't tell what was blocking us.
What got left out, from your side?"
beats.visual_intent: replay the opening moment; the manager delivers the three-part feedback this time, Priya leans in to answer

grounding.claim: a widely taught way to structure feedback is behaviour, impact, then a question that invites the other person's view

narration: Name the behaviour, show the impact, then ask.
Try it on your next one.
beats.visual_intent: presenter returns to camera to close; behind her, a clean version of the now-clear update

grounding.claim: a widely taught way to structure workplace feedback is in three parts, in this order: behaviour, impact, question
